# Compose!

> Excerpt: Students are given four functions and asked to compose them to create the given set of six new functions.

## Problem

Part of the definition of a function is the specification of its [domain](https://undergroundmathematics.org/glossary/domain). The choice of domain may affect the [range](https://undergroundmathematics.org/glossary/range-of-a-function) of the function.

| \(A(x)= x^2-2\) | \(B(x)= 2x+4\) |
| --- | --- |
| \(C(x)= \dfrac{1}{x}\) | \(D(x)= \sqrt{x+2}-2\) |

 What is the largest possible domain for each of the functions

\(A\)

 to

\(D\)

 and what is the corresponding range?

The functions above have been composed in some way to make the following new functions:

| \(f(x)=\dfrac{2}{x}+4\) | \(f(x)=4x^2+16x+14\) |
| --- | --- |
| \(f(x)=\dfrac{1}{2x^2}\) | \(f(x)=x-2\) |
| \(f(x)=\dfrac{1}{4x+12}\) | \(f(x)=x\) |

Can you work out which functions have been composed and in what order to make the new functions?

What are the domain and range for each composition of functions above?

Note that the *composition* might only be defined on a smaller domain than is possible for the function \(f(x)\).

Looking at each composition in turn,

- Can you match it with original functions that have similar features?
- Can you eliminate any of the original functions that cannot possibly be involved in creating it?

**Prompting questions**

## Solution

To find the domain and range for a function, it sometimes helps to sketch its graph.

We can sketch the graph of \(y=x^2\), and \(y=A(x)\) is a translation of it—in which direction?

\(A(x)\) can be evaluated for any input \(x\) so the domain of \(A(x)\) is all real numbers, which can be written as \(x\in\mathbb{R}\). The range is \(A(x)\geq-2\).

**Function \(A(x)= x^2-2\)**

The domain and range are both the full set of real numbers, \(\mathbb{R}\).

**Function \(B(x)= 2x+4\)**

> [figure: graph of y=1 over x — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/compose/images/oneoverx.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

Allowing \(x=0\) would produce an undefined result so we need to restrict the domain to \(x\in\mathbb{R}, x\neq0\). No input value can achieve \(C(x)=0\) so the range is also restricted to the real numbers excluding \(0\).  but it's now fixed.

 This version used to make the image crash into the bottom of the box in PDF

 This version works in both outputs but wastes some space in HTML <cm-columns> <cm-column> Allowing $x=0$ would produce an undefined result so we need to restrict the domain to $x\in\mathbb{R}, x\neq0$. No input value can achieve $C(x)=0$ so the range is also restricted to the real numbers excluding $0$. </cm-column> <cm-column> <cm-image url="images/oneoverx.png" alt-text="graph of y=1 over x" caption=""/> </cm-column> </cm-columns>

**Function \(C(x)= \dfrac{1}{x}\)**

> [figure: graph of root x+2 subtract 2 — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/compose/images/rootxplus2minus2.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record). The graph of this function is a translation of \(y=\sqrt{x}\).

The square root is undefined when \(x+2<0\) so the domain of this function is \(x\ge-2\).

We can evaluate \(D(-2)=-2\) and the square root function always increases as \(x\) increases, so the range is \(D(x)\ge-2\).

 This version used to crash the box in PDF. It wastes less space in HTML but chalk doesn't clear the float so I've had to de-chalk it

 This version works in both outputs but wastes some space in HTML <cm-columns> <cm-column> <cm-chalk> The graph of this function is a translation of $y=\sqrt{x}$. </cm-chalk> The square root is undefined when $x+2<0$ so the domain of this function is $x\ge-2$. We can evaluate $D(-2)=-2$ and the square root function always increases as $x$ increases, so the range is $D(x)\ge-2$. </cm-column> <cm-column> <cm-image url="images/rootxplus2minus2.png" alt-text="graph of root x+2 subtract 2" caption=""/> </cm-column> </cm-columns>

**Function \(D(x)= \sqrt{x+2}-2\)**

Note that the *composition* might only be defined on a smaller domain than is possible for the function \(f(x)\).

We can see that this contains \(\dfrac{1}{x}\), suggesting function \(C\), and the form “\(something+4\)” hints at \(B\) being involved. \(B\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)=\dfrac{2}{x}+4\), giving us \[f(x)= \frac{2}{x}+4= BC(x).\]

The notation \(BC(x)\) is used to mean \(B\bigl(C(x)\bigr)\).

Using \(C(x)\) means the domain is \(x\neq0\) and since \(C(x)\neq0\) we cannot achieve 4 from \(BC(x)\). Hence the range is \(BC(x)\neq 4\). Can you illustrate this with a sketch of \(y=BC(x)\)?

**1.\(\quad f(x)=\dfrac{2}{x}+4\)**

We require a quadratic which leads us straight to \(A\). We don’t want any fractions, so we’re probably going to compose it with the linear function \(B\). Notice that we want the coefficient of \(x^2\) to be \(4\) which we could achieve by squaring \(B\).

We try \((2x+4)^2=4x^2+16x+16\) and see that \[f(x) = 4x^2+16x+14 = AB(x) .\]

We can allow any input value, hence the domain is \(\mathbb{R}\). As \(B(x)\in \mathbb{R}\), it follows that \(AB(x)\) has the same range as \(A(x)\), so \(AB(x)\geq-2\).

**2.\(\quad f(x)={4x^2~+~16x~+~14}\)**

The fraction means we probably need to use \(C\), and the \(x^2\) indicates \(A\), but \(CA(x)=\dfrac{1}{x^2-2}\). We need the coefficient of \(x^2\) in the denominator to be \(2\), so first applying \(B\) before \(C\) will do this and helpfully it will also remove the unwanted \(-2\).

Since \(BA(x)=2(x^2-2)+4=2x^2\) we have \[f(x) =\frac{1}{2x^2} =CBA(x) .\]

To determine the domain and range we note that for \(A\) (which is applied first) the domain is the real numbers and the range is \(A(x)\geq-2\). This becomes the input of \(B\) so \(BA(x)\geq0\). The domain of \(C\) excludes \(x=0\) so we must exclude that output from \(B\). We do this by excluding the input of \(-2\). This means that the domain of \(CBA(x)\) is \(x\ne-2\) and it has range \(CBA(x)>0\).

**3.\(\quad f(x)=\dfrac{1}{2x^2}\)**

Notice that the function \(\sqrt{x^2}\) gives the *positive* square root, so in order for \(DA(x)\) to equal \(x-2\) as required, \(x\) must be non-negative.

This gives \(DA(x)\) the restricted domain of \(x\ge0\). We need to check whether the domain is further restricted by the functions \(D\) and \(A\). The domain of \(A\) is \(\mathbb{R}\) which includes all of \(x\ge0\). Even with the restricted domain, the range is \(A(x) \ge-2\). This becomes the input of \(D\) and matches its domain, so \(DA\) has the same range as \(D\).

The composed function therefore has domain \(x\ge0\) and range \(DA(x) \ge-2\).

 We notice the similarity to the function

\(A(x)\)

, but

\(A\)

 has a quadratic term—how could we cancel that out?

\(D\)

 contains the square root of

\(x+2\)

, so if we apply

\(D\)

 to the output of

\(A\)

 we get

\[\begin{align*} DA(x)&=\sqrt{A(x)+2}-2\\ &=\sqrt{x^2-2+2}-2\\ &=\sqrt{x^2}-2\\ &=|x|-2 . \end{align*}\]

**4.\(\quad f(x)=x-2\)**

We might look at this and think about function \(C\), but we need the input to this to be \(4x+12\) which doesn’t immediately look like any of the other functions.

It might be a good idea to change tack and think what we can generate by composing some of the functions with themselves.

1. Since \(A(x)\) is quadratic \(A^2(x)\) will be quartic. So this is not going to help!  The notation \(A^2(x)\) is used to mean \(A\bigl(A(x)\bigr)\).
2. \(B^2(x)=B(2x+4)=2(2x+4)+4=4x+12\)  That is what we need as input for \(C\) so \[f(x) =\frac{1}{4x+12} =CB^2(x) .\]

The domain and range of \(B\) are the real numbers, \(\mathbb{R}\), but the domain of \(C\) excludes zero so we must exclude \(4x+12=0\) from the input of the composition. Hence its domain is \(x\neq-3\) and its range is \(CB^2(x)\neq0\).

**5.\(\quad f(x)=\dfrac{1}{4x+12}\)**

This is another case of a function composed with itself.

\[f(x) =x =\dfrac{1}{\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)} =C^2(x)\]

We might suppose that the domain and range of \(f(x)=x\) would be the real numbers, but because it was created by composing \(C(x)\) we have to exclude \(x=0\) from both.

Does this in fact mean that \(C^2(x)\) is not the same as the function \(f(x)=x\)?

**6.\(\quad f(x)=x\)**

# Composing gets me nowhere

> Excerpt: This resource is designed to be used as an introduction to self-inverse functions.
Students are asked to sketch a set of functions, work out which ones are self-inverse and find a graphical connection between them.

## Warm-up

If \(f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x}\), for \(x\ne 0\), what is \(ff(x)\)?

By \(ff(x)\) we mean the composition of \(f\) with itself, sometimes written as \(f^2(x)\).

\[ff(x)=f\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)=\frac{1}{\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)}=x\]

The composition of \(f\) with itself is a function whose output is the same as the input value. We call \(f\) a self-inverse function. Can you explain why we use this name?

Note that the composition \(ff(x)\) is undefined at \(x=0\) even though the function \(x\) *is* defined.

**Answer**

Can you find any other functions that behave in this way when composed with themselves?

## Problem

Sketch the following functions and determine which of them are [self-inverse](https://undergroundmathematics.org/glossary/self-inverse-function).

| \(g(x)=\dfrac{x+1}{x-1}\) | \(m(x)=\dfrac{x-1}{x+1}\) |
| --- | --- |
| \(h(x)=8-x\) | \(n(x)=8+x\) |
| \(k(x)=\dfrac{x}{x-1}\) | \(p(x)=x\) |

What do the graphs of the self-inverse functions have in common?

Sketch and find equations for some other self-inverse functions.

## Solution

In order to sketch the graph of \(y=g(x)\) it is helpful to rewrite it as \[y=\frac{x+1}{x-1}=\frac{x-1+2}{x-1} = 1+\frac{2}{x-1} .\] This reveals that the graph is a transformation of \(y=\dfrac{1}{x}\).

> [figure: graph of x+1 over x-1 — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/composing-gets-me-nowhere/images/graph-g.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

We compose \(g(x)\) with itself: \[ gg(x) = g\left( \frac{x+1}{x-1} \right) = \frac{\frac{x+1}{x-1}+1}{\frac{x+1}{x-1}-1} = \frac{x+1+(x-1)}{x+1-(x-1)} = \frac{2x}{2} = x \]

So \(g(x)\) is self-inverse.

Strictly, for \(g\) to be self-inverse, we should check that its range exactly matches its domain since its output is used as its own input in the composition.

What are the domain and range of \(g(x)\)?

**\(g(x)=\dfrac{x+1}{x-1}\)**

By rewriting \(m\) we find that, as for \(g\), its graph is a transformation of \(y=\dfrac{1}{x}\).

so \(m(x)\) is **not** self-inverse.

What is different about \(g\) that makes it self-inverse while \(m\) is not?

 Composing, we find

\[\begin{align*} mm(x) &= m\left( \frac{x-1}{x+1} \right) = \frac{\frac{x-1}{x+1}-1}{\frac{x-1}{x+1}+1}\\ &= \frac{x-1-(x+1)}{x-1+(x+1)} = \frac{-2}{2x} = -\frac{1}{x} , \end{align*}\]

> [figure: graph of x-1 over x+1 — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/composing-gets-me-nowhere/images/graph-m.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

What happens if we compose \(mm(x)\) with itself to make the function \(mmmm(x)\) (which could be written as \(m^4(x)\))?

**\(m(x)=\dfrac{x-1}{x+1}\)**

Of the remaining functions, we find that \(h\), \(k\) and \(p\) are self-inverse.

**Functions \(h\), \(k\), \(n\) and \(p\)**

We have sketched the four self-inverse functions on the same set of axes.

> [figure: sketch of functions g h k and p — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/composing-gets-me-nowhere/images/newimage2.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

We remember that the graphs of any function and its inverse are reflections of one another in the line \(y=x\). So it is no surprise that the graph of each self-inverse function is a reflection of *itself* in \(y=x\).

Can you match up the four functions with their graphs?

By thinking about the reflection property we can see that any straight line parallel to the purple line in the graph above will represent a self-inverse function. Can you write down a generalised form of the equation?

Also, any translation of \(y=\dfrac{1}{x}\) will be self-inverse so long as the origin is transformed to a point on the line \(y=x\). What about stretches, reflections and other transformations?

Can you find any other families of self-inverse functions?

# Domain and range dominoes

> Excerpt: This card sorting activity makes students think carefully about what we mean by the domain and range of a function and how to express them precisely. They will get lots of practise whilst arranging the cards into a loop.

## Warm-up

Describe in words, as accurately as possible, the [domain](https://undergroundmathematics.org/glossary/domain) and [range](https://undergroundmathematics.org/glossary/range-of-a-function) of the functions illustrated here.

> [figure: Graph of square root three x times one minus x which has maximum height 2/3 and intersects the x-axis at 1 — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/domain-and-range-dominoes/images/warm-root3xtimes1minusx.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

*\(f(x)=\sqrt{3x}(1-x)\)*

> [figure: Graph of one over x minus 1, which has a vertical asymptote at x=1 and crosses the y-axis at -1 — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/domain-and-range-dominoes/images/oneoverxminus1.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

*\(f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x-1}\)*

Can you write the domains and ranges using mathematical notation?

The function on the left is undefined for any negative value of \(x\) because of the square root. It is defined at \(x=0\), so we could describe its domain as any real number greater than or equal to zero. \(f(0)=0\) and as \(x\) increases \(f(x)\) increases up to \(\frac{2}{3}\) then decreases. The function’s range is any real number less than or equal to \(\frac{2}{3}\). \[\text{domain: }x\in\mathbb{R}\text{, }x\ge0\quad\text{ range: }f(x)\in\mathbb{R}\text{, }f(x)\le\frac{2}{3}\]

The symbols \(\in\mathbb{R}\) are mathematical notation meaning “is a member of the set of all real numbers”.

The function on the right is defined for all real values of \(x\) except for \(x=1\). Its range is all real numbers greater than zero and all real numbers less than zero. Notice that it is impossible to obtain the output value \(f(x)=0\). \[\text{domain: }x\in\mathbb{R}\text{, }x\ne1\quad\text{ range: }f(x)\in\mathbb{R}\text{, }f(x)\ne0\]

Sometimes, the domain and range might be written in an abbreviated form such as \[\text{domain: }x\ne1\quad\text{ range: }f(x)\ne0 \text{ .}\]

We refer to *real* numbers as opposed to *[imaginary](https://undergroundmathematics.org/glossary/imaginary-number)* or *[complex](https://undergroundmathematics.org/glossary/complex-number)* numbers. You may learn about those elsewhere.

**Check your answers**

## Problem

Match up each function with its domain and range. They form a set of [domino cards](https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/domain-and-range-dominoes/components/cards.pdf) that can be arranged in a sequence.

To turn the sequence into a closed loop, you will need to complete the cards with missing information. A separate sheet containing just those cards is available [here](https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/domain-and-range-dominoes/components/blank-cards.pdf).

| > [figure: graph of x squared plus 1 — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/domain-and-range-dominoes/images/xsquaredplus1.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record). \(f(x)=x^2+1\) | domain: \(x\neq-1\) range: \(f(x)\neq0\) |
| --- | --- |

| > [figure: graph of mod x — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/domain-and-range-dominoes/images/modx.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record). \(f(x)=\|x\|\) | domain: \(x\in \mathbb{R}\) range: \(f(x)\ge1\) |
| --- | --- |

| > [figure: graph of cube root x — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/domain-and-range-dominoes/images/cuberootx.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record). \(f(x)=\sqrt[3]{x}\) | domain: \(x\in \mathbb{R}\) range: \(0\!<\!f(x)\!\le\!1\) |
| --- | --- |

| > [figure: graph of square root x — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/domain-and-range-dominoes/images/sqrtx.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record). \(f(x)=\sqrt{x}\) | domain: \(x\in \mathbb{R}\) range: \(f(x)\ge-1\) |
| --- | --- |

| > [figure: graph of 1 over x — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/domain-and-range-dominoes/images/oneoverx.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record). \(f(x)=\frac{1}{x}\) | domain: \(x\neq0\) range: \(f(x)\ne-1\) |
| --- | --- |

| > [figure: graph of x plus 1 over x — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/domain-and-range-dominoes/images/xplusoneoverx.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record). \(f(x)=x+\frac{1}{x}\) | domain: \(x\neq-1\), \(x\neq1\) range: \(f(x)\le-1\) or \(f(x)>0\) |
| --- | --- |

| > [figure: graph of 1 over x squared — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/domain-and-range-dominoes/images/oneoverxsquared.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record). \(f(x)=\frac{1}{x^2}\) | domain: \(x\in \mathbb{R}\) range: \(f(x)\ge0\) |
| --- | --- |

| > [figure: graph of 1 over x squared plus 1 — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/domain-and-range-dominoes/images/oneoverxsquaredplus1.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record). \(f(x)=\frac{1}{x^2+1}\) | domain: \(x\ge0\) range: \(f(x)\ge0\) |
| --- | --- |

| > [figure: graph of 1 over x squared minus 1 — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/domain-and-range-dominoes/images/oneoverxsquaredminus1.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record). \(f(x)=\frac{1}{x^2-1}\) | domain: \(x>0\) range: \(f(x)>0\) |
| --- | --- |

| > [figure: graph of 1 over 1 plus x — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/domain-and-range-dominoes/images/oneoveroneplusx.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record). \(f(x)=\frac{1}{1+x}\) | domain: \(x\ge0\) range: \(f(x)\le\frac{2}{3}\) |
| --- | --- |

| > [figure: graph of 1 over square root x — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/domain-and-range-dominoes/images/oneoversqrtx.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record). \(f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\) | domain: \(x\in \mathbb{R}\) range: \(f(x)\in \mathbb{R}\) |
| --- | --- |

| > [figure: graph of root 3 x times 1 minus x — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/domain-and-range-dominoes/images/root3xtimes1minusx.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record). \(f(x)=\sqrt{3x}(1-x)\) | domain: \(x\neq0\) range: \(f(x)\neq0\) |
| --- | --- |

| > [figure: blank axes — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/domain-and-range-dominoes/images/blankaxes.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record). \(f(x)=\frac{1}{x}-1\) | domain: range: |
| --- | --- |

| > [figure: blank axes — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/domain-and-range-dominoes/images/blankaxes.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record). \(f(x)=\qquad\qquad\) | domain: range: |
| --- | --- |

## Things you may have noticed

### Unrestricted domains

In this exercise we are using domain to mean all the *possible* values of \(x\). In other contexts, we may artificially restrict the domain of a function. For instance we might only be interested in the function \(f(x)=x^2\) in the domain \(0\le x<2\).

### Similar inequalities

With some of the functions you have to be careful to distinguish between, for instance, \(x>0\) and \(x\ge0\).

### Multiple inequalities

One of the functions has a range that is between \(0\) and \(1\), including \(1\) but not including \(0\). This can be written neatly as \(0<f(x)\le1\).

Another has a range that includes all numbers \(>0\) and all numbers \(\le-1\) but not numbers in between. This has to be written as two separate inequalities.

### Turning points of \(x+\frac{1}{x}\)

Finding the range of \(f(x)=x+\frac{1}{x}\) depends on knowing the value of the function at its turning points (maximum and minimum) and this is not given on the card. There is more than one way to find these values; here are a few.

#### Using calculus

We could differentiate the function and thus find when its gradient is zero.

#### Using an inequality

By substitution we can find that

\(f(1)=2\)

. Is there any positive

\(x\)

value for which

\(f(x)<2\)

? If so,

\[\begin{align*} x+\frac{1}{x}&<2\\ x^2+1&<2x \text{ .} \end{align*}\]

Rearranging and factorising leads to an inequality with no real solutions, so \(2\) must be the minimum value of \(f(x)\) for positive \(x\). The local maximum can be found by symmetry.

When rearranging the inequality, why does it matter that the question specified *positive* \(x\) values?

#### By adding gradients

Notice that \(f(x)\) is the sum of two functions: \(x\) and \(\frac{1}{x}\). So the gradient of \(f(x)\) is the sum of the gradients of \(x\) and \(\frac{1}{x}\) *(it is possible to prove this, but we aren’t going to do so here!)*.

\(y=x\) has gradient \(1\), so the turning points of \(f(x)\) will be where \(y=\frac{1}{x}\) has gradient \(-1\). Can you find the \(x\) values where this happens?

> [figure: scan of dominoes arranged in a loop — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/domain-and-range-dominoes/images/solution-picture-large.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

**Here is one way of arranging the cards**

# Forming functions — defining domains

> Excerpt: For each rule, define several different functions by choosing different domains. How does the choice of domain affect the range of the resulting function?

## Problem

To define a function we need a set of inputs (called the [domain](https://undergroundmathematics.org/glossary/domain)) and some sort of rule for turning inputs into outputs. The set of outputs is called the [range](https://undergroundmathematics.org/glossary/range-of-a-function) of the function.

Here are some rules which tell us what will happen to a given input value, \(x\).

> [figure: rule A x maps to x squared minus 2, rule B x maps to x minus x cubed, rule C x maps to 4 over x squared minus 4, rule D x maps to the square root of x plus 2 — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/forming-functions-defining-domains/images/functions3.svg`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

For each rule,

- Define a function by choosing a domain. Now define another function by choosing a different domain.
- For each function you have defined, state the corresponding range of the function.
- Sketch graphs of the functions you have defined.

For each rule,

- What is the largest possible domain you can define within the real numbers?
- What is the smallest possible domain that will define a function with the largest possible range?

## Things you might have tried

There are many possible functions that you could define in each case. We will illustrate some of these ideas using rule \(A.\)

We could define a function using rule \(A\) and letting \(x\) be any real number. We could write this function as \[A : x \mapsto x^2-2, \quad x\in \mathbb{R}.\] The range is all real numbers greater than or equal to \(-2\), which we can write as \(A(x)\in \mathbb{R}\) with \(A(x) \geq -2\).

We could also define a function by restricting \(x\) to be a real number that is greater than or equal to \(1\) but less than \(4\). We could write this as \[A : x \mapsto x^2-2, \quad x\in \mathbb{R}, \; 1 \leq x <4.\] This time, the range is \(A(x)\in \mathbb{R},\) \(-1 \leq A(x) < 14\).

Alternatively, we could restrict \(x\) to being an integer greater than \(-3\), which would give the following function \[A : x \mapsto x^2-2, \quad x\in \mathbb{Z},\; x> -3.\] For this third function, \(A(x)\in \mathbb{Z}\), with \(A(x)\) always \(2\) less than a square number, i.e. \(A(x) \in \{ -2, -1, 2, 7, 14, 23, \ldots\}\).

> [figure: Three graphs of A(x) for different domains. The first is a simple parabola, the second is a section, and the third is a set of points described on the parabola. — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/forming-functions-defining-domains/images/combinedafunctions.svg`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

Note the open and closed circles at the ends of the line in the second graph, indicating whether or not the end point is included in the domain.

**Sketch graphs**

For each rule,

- What is the function with the largest possible domain within the real numbers?

Rules \(A\) and \(B\) are defined for all real inputs, so the largest possible domain would be, for instance, \[A: x \mapsto x^2-2, \quad x\in \mathbb{R}.\]

In contrast, there are values of \(x\) for which rules \(C\) and \(D\) are undefined. For instance the largest possible domain of \(C\) would be, \[C: x\mapsto \dfrac{4}{x^2-4}, \quad x\in \mathbb{R}, \; x\neq \pm2.\]

For each rule,

- What is the smallest possible domain that will define a function with the largest possible range?

Thinking about our three suggested functions for \(A\) above, we found the ranges were as follows.

| Function | Domain | Range |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | \(x\in \mathbb{R}\) | \(A(x)\in \mathbb{R}\), \(A(x)\geq -2\) |
| 2 | \(x\in \mathbb{R}\), \(1 \leq x < 4\) | \(A(x)\in \mathbb{R}\), \(-1 \leq x < 14\) |
| 3 | \(x\in \mathbb{Z}\), \(x > -3\) | \(A(x) \in \{ -2, -1, 2, 7, 14, 23, \ldots\}\) |

Out of these three, function 1 has the largest range. Its range includes all the values in the other two ranges and other values too.

In the case of rule \(A\), the largest possible range results from the function with the largest possible domain.

Is it true in general that if we make the domain of a function as large as possible, we also make the range as large as possible?

But can we obtain the same range with a smaller domain?

For function 1, it is possible to find two different values of \(x\) which give the same value of \(A(x)\), for example, \(A(-1)=A(1)\). So we could remove one of these input values from the domain without changing the range.

We can restrict the domain of \(A(x)\) to be \(x\in \mathbb{R}\), \(x\geq 0\), and the range will still be \(A(x)\geq -2\), as required. What happens if we make the domain any smaller?

Another way would be to define \(A(x)\) for \(x\in \mathbb{R}\), \(x<-5\) or \(0\leq x \leq 5\). What would the graph of this function look like? What other domains could you have which still give you the same range?

Which of these ideas could be applied to functions which are defined using the other rules?

Are there any of the rules for which the only way to achieve the maximum possible range is to define it on the maximum possible domain? What could you say about such functions?

As we’ll see later, this idea of restricting the domain without limiting the range becomes important when we look at [making inverse functions](https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/making-inverse-functions).

# Invertibles

> Excerpt: Pair up the functions so that each one is with its inverse function; match the pairs of functions with graphs and sketch in the missing curves.

## Problem

- Put these functions in pairs – each one with its [inverse](https://undergroundmathematics.org/glossary/inverse-function). One function is missing so you’ll need to fill in the blank card.
- Pull down the bottom edge of the card sort area to reveal the graphs of some of the functions. Match up the functions with their graphs and draw in the graphs of their inverse functions.

\(a(x)=x^2-2\),
 \(x\ge0\)

\(b(x)=(x-2)^2+1\),
 \(x\ge2\)

\(c(x)=(x-2)^2+1\),
 \(x\le2\)

\(d(x)=1+\sqrt{x-2}\),
 \(x\ge2\)

\(e(x)=2-\sqrt{x-1}\),
 \(x\ge1\)

\(f(x)={}\)
 \(\ \)

\(g(x)=\sqrt{x+2}\),
 \(x\ge-2\)

\(h(x)=2+\sqrt{x-1}\),
 \(x\ge1\)

\(p(x)=\dfrac{x}{1+x}\), \(x\ne-1\)

\(q(x)=\dfrac{-x}{1+x}\), \(x\ne-1\)

\(r(x)=\dfrac{x+2}{x+1}\), \(x\ne-1\)

\(s(x)=\dfrac{-x}{1+x}\), \(x\ne-1\)

\(t(x)=\dfrac{x}{1-x}\), \(x\ne1\)

\(u(x)=\vphantom{\dfrac{x+1}{x+1}}\)

**Now try these**

## Solution

Put these functions in pairs – each one with its inverse. One function is missing so you’ll need to fill in the blank card.

Three of the first set of functions are quadratics in completed square form and four involve square roots. We noticed that functions \(a\) and \(g\) are simpler than the others so we looked at those first.

\(a(x)=x^2-2\),
 \(x\ge0\)

\(g(x)=\sqrt{x+2}\),
 \(x\ge-2\)

To find the inverse of \(a(x)\), we rearrange the equation \(y=a(x)\) to make \(x\) the subject. \[y=x^2-2 \quad\implies\quad x^2=y+2 \quad\implies\quad x=\pm\sqrt{y+2}\] To resolve the \(\pm\) ambiguity, note that the definition of \(a(x)\) specifies the [domain](https://undergroundmathematics.org/glossary/domain) \(x\ge0\). So we must require the positive square root. The function \(a(x)\) is defined for all positive values of \(x\) so \(y\) can take any value greater than or equal to \(-2\).

So now changing the input from \(y\) to \(x\) we have the inverse function, \(a^{-1}(x)=\sqrt{x+2}\) defined on the domain \(x\ge-2\). This is the same as \(g(x)\) and we can say that \(g(x)\) is the inverse of \(a(x)\).

For more about the process of finding inverses, see [Making inverse functions](https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/making-inverse-functions).

What would the inverse function be if instead we had \(a(x)\) defined only for \(x\le0\)?

Alternatively, we could verify that \(a\) and \(g\) are inverses by evaluating their composition. \[ag(x) = a(g(x)) = (g(x))^2-2 = (x+2)-2 = x\] This almost confirms it, but we have to think a bit harder to make sure the domains are correct. For what values of \(x\) is \(ag(x)\) defined?

For them to be a pair of inverse functions we also require that \(ga(x)=x\) over a suitable domain.

What are the [ranges](https://undergroundmathematics.org/glossary/range-of-a-function) of \(a(x)\) and \(g(x)\)? How are the domains and ranges of the two functions related?

The graph of \(y=a(x)\) will be a parabola with vertex at \((0,-2)\) but restricted to \(x\) being positive. There is no such graph on the sheet.

The graph of \(y=g(x)\) is a positive square-root graph starting at \((-2,0)\). This is on graph (2), so we can sketch in the graph of \(y=a(x)\) on the same axes.

> [figure: graph of functions a and g — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/invertibles/images/graph-ga.svg`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

**Graphs**

Having had to think about the domains, we next noticed that \(b(x)\) and \(c(x)\) differ *only* in their domains…

\(b(x)=(x-2)^2+1\),
 \(x\ge2\)

\(h(x)=2+\sqrt{x-1}\),
 \(x\ge1\)

\(c(x)=(x-2)^2+1\),
 \(x\le2\)

\(e(x)=2-\sqrt{x-1}\),
 \(x\ge1\)

Rearranging \(y=b(x)\) we have \[x=2\pm\sqrt{y-1}\] but \(x\ge2\) so we need the positive square root here, and as \(x\) increases from \(2\), \(y\) increases from \(1\). Hence we have \[b^{-1}(x)=2+\sqrt{x-1}, \ x\ge1\] which matches function \(h(x)\).

Similarly, rearranging

\(y=c(x)\)

\[x=2\pm\sqrt{y-1}\]

but for

\(c(x)\)

we have

\(x\le2\)

so

\[\begin{align*} c^{-1}(x)&=2-\sqrt{x-1}, \ x\ge1\\ &= e(x). \end{align*}\]

You might have expected a difference only in the domains to result in the inverses differing only in their ranges. But instead we have different functions.

The graph of \(y=h(x)\) appears on graph (1) and \(y=c(x)\) is on graph (4).

> [figure: graph of functions b and h — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/invertibles/images/graph-jb.svg`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

> [figure: graph of functions c and e — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/invertibles/images/graph-ce.svg`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

What do you notice about the pairs of graphs?

**Graphs**

\(d(x)=1+\sqrt{x-2}\),
 \(x\ge2\)

\(f(x)={}\)
 \(\ \)

Rearranging \(y=d(x)\) we have \[x=(y-1)^2+2\] which means that \[d^{-1}(x)=(x-1)^2+2.\]

To find the domain of \(d^{-1}(x)\), consider that as \(x\) increases from \(2\), \(d(x)\) increases from \(1\). So the inverse function will be defined only for \(x\ge1\). Hence \(d(x)\) is paired with \[f(x)=(x-1)^2+2, \ x\ge1.\]

The graph of \(y=d^{-1}(x)\) appears on graph (3).

> [figure: graph of function d and its inverse — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/invertibles/images/graph-dd1.svg`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

**Graphs**

---

The second set are all rational functions. The only one that looks different is \(r(x)\) but it is hard to predict how any of them behave without doing some work, so we started with \(p(x)\).

\(p(x)=\dfrac{x}{1+x}\), \(x\ne-1\)

\(t(x)=\dfrac{x}{1-x}\), \(x\ne1\)

To find the inverse of

\(p(x)\)

we want to rearrange its equation to make

\(x\)

the subject. Here are two different ways of doing that.

\[\begin{align*} y &= \frac{x}{1+x} \\ y+yx &= x \\ yx-x &= -y \\ x(y-1) &= -y \\ x &= \frac{-y}{y-1} \end{align*}\]

\[\begin{align} y=\frac{x}{1+x} &= \frac{1+x-1}{1+x} = 1-\frac{1}{1+x} \label{eq:p-hyperbola}\\ \implies\quad \frac{1}{1+x} &= 1-y \notag\\ \implies\quad x &= \frac{1}{1-y}-1 \label{eq:t-hyperbola}\\ &= \frac{y}{1-y} \notag \end{align}\]

And so we have the inverse function, \[p^{-1}(x) = \frac{x}{1-x} = t(x).\]

We get to the same result, but you might find the second method and equations \(\eqref{eq:p-hyperbola}\) and \(\eqref{eq:t-hyperbola}\) more informative when it comes to sketching the graphs.

In each case the domain is specified to exclude the value of \(x\) where the fraction is undefined.

Equation \(\eqref{eq:p-hyperbola}\) indicates that the graph of \(y=p(x)\) is a \(1/x\) hyperbola turned upside down and translated left by \(1\) and up by \(1\). It appears on graph (6).

We have \(t(x)=-\frac{1}{x-1}-1\) so its graph is an upside down hyperbola translated right and down.

> [figure: graph of functions p and t — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/invertibles/images/graph-pt.svg`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

**Graphs**

\(q(x)=\dfrac{-x}{1+x}\), \(x\ne-1\)

\(s(x)=\dfrac{-x}{1+x}\), \(x\ne-1\)

Rewriting and rearranging as above, we have

\[\begin{align*} y= q(x) &= \frac{-(1+x)+1}{1+x} = -1+\frac{1}{1+x} \\ \implies\quad x &= \frac{1}{1+y}-1 \end{align*}\]

and so \[q^{-1}(x) = \frac{1}{1+x}-1 = \frac{-x}{1+x} = q(x) = s(x).\]

The functions

\(q\)

and

\(q^{-1}\)

are identical which means that this is a

.

What does this imply about the composition \(qq(x)\) or \(q(q(x))\)?

The graph of \(y=q(x)\) is a \(1/x\) hyperbola translated left by \(1\) and down by \(1\). It appears on graph (5).

> [figure: graph of functions self-inverse function q — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/invertibles/images/graph-qs.svg`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

The previous graphs have shown paired functions as reflections of one another. What has happened to this pair?

**Graphs**

\(r(x)=\dfrac{x+2}{x+1}\), \(x\ne-1\)

\(u(x)=\vphantom{\dfrac{x+1}{x+1}}\)

As before we have

\[\begin{align*} r(x) = \frac{x+1+1}{x+1} &= 1+\frac{1}{x+1} \\ \implies\quad r^{-1}(x) = u(x) &= \frac{1}{x-1}-1 \quad\text{for }x\ne1 \end{align*}\]

The graph of \(y=r(x)\) does not appear, but \(y=r^{-1}(x)\) is a \(1/x\) hyperbola translated right by \(1\) and down by \(1\). It appears on graph (7).

> [figure: graph of function r and its inverse — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/invertibles/images/graph-rr1.svg`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

**Graphs**

---

### Things you might have noticed

- In each case, the graphs of a function and its inverse are mirror images of one another in the line \(y=x\).
- The graphs of self-inverse functions are symmetrical about the line \(y=x\).
- The domain of a one-to-one function \(f\) is the same as the range of its inverse \(f^{-1}\) and the range of \(f\) is the same as the domain of \(f^{-1}\).
- In these examples, we have chosen a domain for each function that is as big as possible whilst allowing the function to have an inverse.
  - For the quadratic functions, we chose one half or the other so that the function was [one-to-one](https://undergroundmathematics.org/glossary/injective) rather than many-to-one.
  - For the rational functions, we chose domains that excluded only the problematic values where the functions are undefined (corresponding to vertical asymptotes).
- You could define functions with the same equations on different domains. They could still be inverted so long as they were one-to-one.

# It's a matter of perspective

> Excerpt: This resource asks students to find the equation of a parabola given three points. It can be used as a follow-on from 'Name that graph again', and it introduces a wider range of transformations than those previously encountered.

## Problem

We would like to find an equation for this parabola in the form \(y=f(x)\).

> [figure: Upward facing parabola passing through the points (0,5), (2,1) and (4,13) — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/its-a-matter-of-perspective/images/parabola-2.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

What ways come to mind straight away?

## A certain point of view

Click on the *Animate* button in the applet below or move the slider.

> [interactive embed (geogebra-iframe): //www.geogebratube.org/material/iframe/id/kgWsjQfY/width/600/height/400/border/888888/rc/false/ai/false/sdz/false/smb/false/stb/false/stbh/false/ld/false/sri/true/asb/false/at/html5] — not part of the text import; see the source page.

[Download GeoGebra file](https://www.geogebratube.org/material/download/format/file/id/kgWsjQfY)

What is happening in the animation as the value of \(u\) increases from \(0\) to \(1\)?

As \(u\) increases, the points \((0,5)\) and \((2,1)\) are moved in such a way that their \(x\)-coordinates stay the same but their \(y\)-coordinates smoothly change to \(0\). They are transformed to \((0,0)\) and \((2,0)\).

The red dashed line is drawn passing through the two points described above. This line becomes horizontal (and lies on the \(x\)-axis) when \(u=1\).

The original parabola is transformed so that it always passes through these two points. It appears to remain as a parabola.

The point \(C\) marked on the parabola remains fixed throughout.

**An answer**

Which characteristics of the parabola are being preserved and which are being changed?

The curve does remain as a parabola as \(u\) increases, so we could say that its “parabolic” shape stays the same. Its orientation remains upward facing.

However, it is transformed so that when \(u=1\) it passes through the points \((0,0)\) and \((2,0)\) rather than the points \((0,5)\) and \((2,1)\). The original parabola does not intersect the \(x\)-axis but the transformed one does.

**An answer**

How can we describe the transformation that is happening to the parabola?

Each point on the parabola is being transformed in the same way as each point on the straight line.

The equation of the original straight line can be written as \(y=5-2x\). As \(u\) increases, we are gradually subtracting from its \(y\) values until when \(u=1\) the equation of the line has become \(y=0\). At this stage, we have therefore subtracted \((5-2x)\) from the \(y\) value of each point on the line.

This type of transformation is called a [shear](https://undergroundmathematics.org/glossary/shear); in this case, it is a shear parallel to the \(y\)-axis. A shear is a particular example of an [affine transformation](https://undergroundmathematics.org/glossary/affine-transformation).

 Similarly, if we write the equation of the original parabola as

\(y=f(x)\)

 and subtract

\((5-2x)\)

 when

\(u=1\)

, we can say that the transformed parabola has equation

\[\begin{equation} y=f(x)-(5-2x).\label{eq1} \end{equation}\]

**An answer**

What can we say about the transformed parabola?

where \(K\) is some constant.

 We can see that the transformed parabola intersects the

\(x\)

-axis at

\(x=0\)

 and

\(x=2\)

, so its equation can be written as

\[\begin{equation} y=Kx(x-2),\label{eq2} \end{equation}\]

**An answer**

Can we use the transformed parabola to find the equation of the original parabola, \(y=f(x)\)?

We saw above \(\eqref{eq1}\) that the transformed parabola has equation \(y=f(x)-(5-2x)\), and also \(\eqref{eq2}\) that it can be written as \(y=Kx(x-2)\). Therefore \[f(x)-(5-2x)=Kx(x-2),\] and we can rearrange this to get \[f(x)=5-2x+Kx(x-2).\]

and the equation of the original parabola is \[y = 2x^2-6x+5.\]

 We can find the value of

\(K\)

 by using the third given point on the original parabola

\((4,13)\)

:

\[13 = 5-2\times4+4K(4-2)\]

 and solving this gives

\(K = 2\)

. Thus

\[\begin{align*} f(x) &= 5-2x+2x(x-2)\\ &= 2x^2-6x+5 \end{align*}\]

**An answer**

A point \(C\) is marked on the diagram. What happens to the point \(C\) as \(u\) varies and what condition must the point \(C\) satisfy?

**A final thought**

# Making inverse functions

> Excerpt: Here we revisit the algebraic process of finding an inverse for a function, and explore the importance of specifying the domain and when we need to restrict the domain in order to make a function invertible.

## Function machines

Starting with a function \[f(x)=2x+1\] defined for \(x\) as any real number, we can represent it as a function machine. We put \(x\) in at the left and get \(f(x)\) out at the right.

> [figure: function machine doing times 2 then plus 1 — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/making-inverse-functions/images/function-machine.svg`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

The inverse function, \(f^{-1}\), is such that if we put in \(f(x)\) we’ll get out \(x\). Fill in the boxes below so that if you put in \(2x+1\) at the right, you get \(x\) out at the left.

> [figure: blank function machine converting 2x+1 into x — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/making-inverse-functions/images/inverse-blank-machine.svg`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

To find out what the inverse function is, use the same machine, put in \(x\) at the right and see what comes out at the left. The expression that comes out at the left is equal to \(f^{-1}(x)\).

In other words, \(f^{-1}(y)\) is what we get by rearranging \(\eqref{eq:f}\) to make \(x\) the subject. We can then simply replace each \(y\) with an \(x\) to find \(f^{-1}(x)\).

\[2x=y-1 \quad\text{so}\quad x=\frac{1}{2}(y-1). \quad\text{Therefore}\quad f^{-1}(x)=\frac{1}{2}(x-1)=\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{2}.\]

**Solution**

 If we had written

\(y=2x+1\)

, then we would have

\[\begin{equation} y=f(x). \label{eq:f} \end{equation}\]

 The second function machine above tells us that putting

\(y\)

 into

\(f^{-1}\)

 we get out

\(x\)

, so

\[\begin{equation} x=f^{-1}(y). \label{eq:f-1} \end{equation}\]

 Complete the following.

\[\begin{align*} y &= 2x+1 \\ \\ 2x &= \\ \\ x &= \qquad\qquad\qquad = f^{-1}(y) \\ \\ \text{Therefore}\quad f^{-1}(x) &= \end{align*}\]

**Rearranging**

Find the inverse of each of these functions, either by drawing a function machine or by rearranging the formula.

1. \(f(x) = 3x-2,\quad x\in\mathbb{R}\)
2. \(f(x) = x^3-1,\quad x\in\mathbb{R}\)

The symbols \(x\in\mathbb{R}\) define the domain of the function and mean \(x\) can be any real number.

1. \(y=3x-2 \quad\implies\quad x=\frac{1}{3}(y+2) \quad\implies\quad f^{-1}(x)=\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{2}{3},\; x\in\mathbb{R}\)
2. \(y=x^3-1 \quad\implies\quad x=\sqrt[3]{y+1} \quad\implies\quad f^{-1}(x)=\sqrt[3]{x+1},\; x\in\mathbb{R}\)

**Solution**

**Now try these**

Note we have chosen functions that can be written as simple function machines. There are many functions which cannot be written like this and many which cannot be inverted algebraically. Can you think of some examples?

## Defining domains

What is \(x\) if \(x^2-2=7\)?

What if you also knew that \(x\geq 0\)?

If \(x^2-2=7\) then \(x\) could be \(3\) or \(-3\), but by restricting \(x\) to \(x\geq 0\), we ensure there is a single solution to the equation \(x^2-2=7\). (Of course, we could have restricted \(x\) in other ways to ensure that there was a single solution.)

**Answer**

#### The need for one-to-one

Let’s think about this quadratic problem in terms of functions and consider the function \(f(x)=x^2-2\) where \(x\) can be any real number. The [domain](https://undergroundmathematics.org/glossary/domain) of \(f\) is \(\mathbb{R}\) and the [range](https://undergroundmathematics.org/glossary/range-of-a-function) is the [interval](https://undergroundmathematics.org/glossary/interval-notation) \([-2,\infty)\) or in other words \(f(x)\ge-2\).

The function is [many-to-one](https://undergroundmathematics.org/glossary/many-to-one), which you can see from the graph of \(y=f(x)\) below. For instance, the inputs \(3\) and \(-3\) both give the same output value, namely \(7\).

The inverse function, \(f^{-1}(x)\), would be one that ‘undoes’ the effects of \(f(x)\), but what value should we get for \(f^{-1}(7)\)? We would want it to provide both values, \(3\) and \(-3\), making it a one-to-many relation but we do not consider things with more than one output to be functions.

\[y=x^2-2 \quad\implies\quad x^2=y+2 \quad\implies\quad x=\pm\sqrt{y+2}\] This seems to imply that \[f^{-1}(x)=\pm\sqrt{x+2}\] but the \(\pm\) indicates one-to-many behaviour, so \(f^{-1}\) is not actually a function.

**What happens if we try to invert the function algebraically?**

See the resource [What relation are you?](https://undergroundmathematics.org/thinking-about-functions/what-relation-are-you) for more about many-to-one and one-to-many relations.

#### Restricting the domain

If we define a new function, \(g(x)\), with the same rule as \(f(x)\) but with its domain restricted to \([0,\infty)\), then this function *is* one-to-one (also known as [injective](https://undergroundmathematics.org/glossary/injective)).

> [figure: graphs showing f of x with domain R and g of x with domain x greater than or equal to zero — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/making-inverse-functions/images/quadraticexamples.svg`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

This means that

\(g\)

is invertible and we can write its inverse function as

\[g^{-1}(x) = \sqrt{x+2},\quad x\ge-2.\]

How did I know to use the positive rather than the negative square root?

> [figure: graph showing g-inverse of x — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/making-inverse-functions/images/graph-g-1.svg`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

Notice that,

- Function \(g\) has the same range as \(f\) so any value that can be obtained as output from \(f\) can also be obtained from \(g\).
- The domain of \(g^{-1}(x)\) is \([-2,\infty)\), which is the range of \(g(x)\).
- The range of \(g^{-1}(x)\) is \([0,\infty)\), which is the domain of \(g(x)\).

We chose to restrict the domain of \(g\) to \([0,\infty)\), but we could instead have chosen to restrict it to \((-\infty,0]\). What would the graph of \(y=g(x)\) then look like? What would its range have been? Would it be invertible?

Another function is defined as \(h(x)=x^2-2, \ 1\le x\le4\). What is its range and what is its inverse function?

This alternative \(g\) has range \([-2,\infty)\), which is the same as before. It is still one-to-one, but now we see that we need to take the *negative* square root to find the inverse of \(g\), because the domain of \(g\) is \((-\infty,0]\). \[y=g(x)=x^2-2 \quad\implies\quad x^2=y+2 \quad\implies\quad x=-\sqrt{y+2}\] and therefore \[g^{-1}(x)=-\sqrt{x+2}\]

> [figure: graph of g with domain x less than or equal to zero — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/making-inverse-functions/images/alternative-g.svg`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

Notice that the domain of \(h^{-1}\) is the range of \(h\) and vice versa.

 For the function

\(h\)

, since it has domain

\([1,4]\)

, we will have to take the positive square root to find its inverse.

\[\begin{align*} h(x) &=x^2-2,\quad 1\le x\le4; \quad \text{range: }[-1,14] \\ h^{-1}(x) &=\sqrt{x+2},\quad-1\le x\le14; \quad \text{range: }[1,4] \end{align*}\]

**Answers**

#### Definitions

When we say that two functions, \(f\) and \(f^{-1}\), are inverses we mean that each one “undoes” the action of the other. Applying one and then the other (either way round) will take us back to our starting value.

Algebraically we can say that,

- \(f^{-1}(f(x))=x\) for all values of \(x\) in the domain of \(f\), and
- \(f(f^{-1}(y))=y\) for all values of \(y\) in the domain of \(f^{-1}\).

In order to achieve this, not only must \(f\) be one-to-one on its entire domain, but also the domain of \(f^{-1}\) must be the same as the range of \(f\) and vice-versa. Below, we shall explore why this is.

There is a concept of a one-sided inverse, where one of the above bullet points is true but not the other. However, we are only going to consider cases where they are inverses both ways round.

#### Matching domains and ranges

#### Function machines

We can represent the composition of a function and its inverse as a function machine.

> [figure: function machine diagram showing f then f inverse and another the other way round — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/making-inverse-functions/images/function-machine-inverses.svg`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

In the middle of the first diagram, the output of \(f\) becomes the input of \(f^{-1}\), and so the range of \(f\) must match the domain of \(f^{-1}\). The second machine shows that the domain of \(f\) must match the range of \(f^{-1}\).

#### Graphs

Another way to think about this is to consider the graph above of the function \(y=g(x)\). Starting at a value of \(x\) in the domain of \(g\) we find \(y\) by tracking vertically from the \(x\)-axis to the curve then horizontally to the \(y\)-axis.

As \(g^{-1}\) is the inverse, the same graph also represents \(x=g^{-1}(y)\). Starting at a \(y\) value on the \(y\)-axis we track the same path in reverse to find our \(x\) value. As it is the same graph, the range of possible outputs from \(g\) must be the same as the domain of possible inputs to \(g^{-1}\) and vice-versa.

#### A diagrammatic approach

We can draw a diagram to represent the function \(f\), as we did in [What relation are you?](https://undergroundmathematics.org/thinking-about-functions/what-relation-are-you).

> [figure: Two ovals each containing five dots, each dot in the left oval is joined to to a different dot in the right oval by an arrow — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/making-inverse-functions/images/f-diagram.svg`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

The dots on the left represent the domain of \(f\) and as \(f\) is a one-to-one function, there is at most one arrow coming into each dot on the right. We have also chosen to make the right hand set be exactly the range of \(f\), so *every* dot has an arrow coming into it.

What would the diagram for \(f^{-1}\) look like, and how does this show that the domain of \(f^{-1}\) is the range of \(f\) and vice versa?

The arrows are all reversed to get the inverse function:

> [figure: The same diagram as above, but with all of the arrows reversed — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/making-inverse-functions/images/finv-diagram.svg`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

It is clear from these diagrams that the domain of \(f\), which is the left set, is the range of \(f^{-1}\), while the range of \(f\), which is the right set, is the domain of \(f^{-1}\).

**Solution**

## Invertible sort

Below are graphs of twelve functions. Some are invertible on the domain shown and some are not. Can you sort them out?

You might think about…

- is the function one-to-one or many-to-one?
- how could you restrict the domain to make an invertible function?
- can you find a restricted domain that makes an invertible function with the same range as the unrestricted function?

Graph 1 > [figure:  — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/making-inverse-functions/images/new2b.svg`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

# Name that graph again

> Excerpt: Students think about different ways in which they can determine the equation of a parabola given the coordinates of three points on the curve.

## Problem

In how many ways can you identify an equation for this parabola?

> [figure: Upward facing parabola passing through the points (0,4.5), (1.5,1.5), and (2,4.5) — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/name-that-graph-again/images/parabola-1.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

How might considering this diagram help?

> [figure: Shows the previous parabola translated down by 4.5 so that it now passes through the points (0,0), (1.5,-3) and (2,0) — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/name-that-graph-again/images/parabola-1a.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

What do you know about the red parabola?

What has the red parabola got to do with the blue one?

**Have you thought about…?**

## Student starting points

In how many ways can you identify an equation for this parabola?

> [figure: Upward facing parabola passing through the points (0,4.5), (1.5,1.5), and (2,4.5) — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/name-that-graph-again/images/parabola-1.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

Below you will find four ways in which students have started to tackle this problem. For each approach, try to work out what they were doing and attempt to continue their work to reach a solution.

> [figure: Upward facing parabola passing through the points (0,4.5), (1.5,1.5), and (2,4.5) — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/name-that-graph-again/images/student-1c.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

- What is this student doing?
- Why are they doing that?
- What could they do next?

**Student 1**

> [figure: A photo of student work showing the vertical line of symmetry of the parabola — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/name-that-graph-again/images/student-3.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

- What is this student doing?
- Why are they doing that?
- What could they do next?

**Student 2**

> [figure: A photo of student work showing the original curve translated 2 units vertically downwards — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/name-that-graph-again/images/student-2a.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

- What is this student doing?
- Why are they doing that?
- What could they do next?

**Student 3**

Student 4 has taken a more unusual approach. This approach is better considered after having explored one or more of the first three starting points.

> [figure: A photo of student work showing the gradient at two points on the parabola — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/name-that-graph-again/images/student-4.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=2ax+b\]

- What is this student doing?
- Why are they doing that?
- What could they do next?

You might like to think about how the approach taken by this student is connected to the ideas in [Parabella](https://undergroundmathematics.org/quadratics/parabella).

**Student 4**

## Solution

In how many ways can you identify the equation of this parabola?

> [figure: Upward facing parabola passing through the points (0,4.5), (1.5,1.5), and (2,4.5) — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/name-that-graph-again/images/parabola-1.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

In [Name that graph](https://undergroundmathematics.org/quadratics/name-that-graph) we thought about the three formats in which we can write a quadratic equation. We explored some of the ways in which the equation of a parabola could be determined in each of these three forms and the relative efficiency of each.

Here we have three coordinates specified on the parabola, but because the graph is not plotted accurately with a background grid, we cannot read any additional points from the diagram.

We could of course go through the laborious process of forming three equations, one from each of the specified points on the parabola, in \(a,b, c\) and solve them simultaneously. This will give an equation in the form \(y=ax^2+bx+c\).

We can eliminate \(b\) by doing \(1.5 \times\)\(\eqref{eq:5}\) - \(2\times\)\(\eqref{eq:4}\) so that we have, \[6 = 1.5a\] giving \[a = 4.\]

Substituting the value of \(a\) back into equation \(\eqref{eq:5}\) we have \[0 = 16 + 2b\] and so \[b = -8.\]

The equation of the parabola is therefore \[y = 4x^2 - 8x + 4.5.\]

 Using each of the three specified coordinates in turn we obtain three equations:

\[\begin{align} 4.5 = c\label{eq:1} \\ 1.5 = 2.25a + 1.5b + c\label{eq:2}\\ 4.5 = 4a + 2b + c\label{eq:3} \end{align}\]

 Substituting the value of

\(c\)

 from equation

\(\eqref{eq:1}\)

 into equations

\(\eqref{eq:2}\)

 and

\(\eqref{eq:3}\)

 and simplifying we have

\[\begin{align} -3 = 2.25a + 1.5b\label{eq:4} \\ 0 = 4a + 2b\label{eq:5} \end{align}\]

**Approach 1**

We could instead locate the line of symmetry and use this to find the equation of the parabola in completed square form.

We are given two horizontally aligned points on the parabola, \((0, 4.5)\) and \((2, 4.5)\). The line of symmetry will therefore be a vertical line located midway between these two points, i.e. the line \(x = 1\).

This means that the parabola can be written in the form \[y=a(x-1)^2 + e.\]

Solving simultaneously, by first eliminating \(e\) from equation \(\eqref{eq:7}\), we have \[3 = 0.75a = \frac{3}{4} a\] and so \[a = 4.\]

Notice that converting the decimal into a fraction makes it easier to see the solution.

Substituting the value of \(a\) back into equation \(\eqref{eq:7}\) we find that \(e=0.5\).

So we now know that the equation of the parabola is \[y = 4(x-1)^2 + 0.5.\]

It is sensible to check that this agrees with the equation obtained from approach \(1\).

Expanding we have \[y = 4x^2 - 8x + 4 + 0.5\] which simplifies to \[y=4x^2 - 8x + 4.5\] as expected.

 Substituting the points

\((0, 4.5)\)

 and

\((1.5, 1.5)\)

 into this equation we have the two equations:

\[\begin{align} 4.5 = a + e\label{eq:7} \\ 1.5 = 0.25a + e\label{eq:8} \end{align}\]

**Approach 2**

Making use of the diagram in “Have you thought about…” we could find the equation by considering a translation of the original parabola.

> [figure: Shows the previous parabola translated down by 4.5 so that it now passes through the points (0,0), (1.5,-3) and (2,0) — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/name-that-graph-again/images/parabola-1a.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

We can find the equation of the red parabola in factorised form because we can see the location of the two \(x\)-intercepts: \[y=ax(x-2).\]

Substituting the third point on this translated parabola, \((1.5, -3)\) into the equation we can find the value of \(a\): \[-3 = 0.75a = \frac{3}{4} a\] and so \[a = 4.\]

So the equation of the red, translated parabola is \[y=4x(x-2).\] If we call the original blue parabola \(f(x)\) then the red parabola is \(f(x) - 4.5\).

We now have that \[f(x) - 4.5 = 4x(x-2).\] Rearranging we have that \[f(x) = 4x(x-2) + 4.5\] and then expanding we get \[f(x) = 4x^2 - 8x + 4.5.\] So the equation of the blue parabola is \[y = 4x^2 - 8x + 4.5\] as before.

**Approach 3**

# Order! Order!

> Excerpt: Students are asked to think about and describe combinations of graph transformations with a view to seeing when the order matters and when it does not.

## Warm-up

Here is a graph of a function, \(f(x)\).

> [figure: Cubic shaped graph crossing the x-axis at -1 and touching it at 2, and crossing the y-axis at 4 — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/order-order/images/original-fx.svg`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

For each of the following transformations, sketch the transformed graph and write its equation in terms of \(f\).

Translation by \(\begin{pmatrix}-2\\0\end{pmatrix}\)

Translation by \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\-4\end{pmatrix}\)

Stretch by factor \(3\) parallel to \(x\)

Stretch by factor \(\frac{1}{2}\) parallel to \(y\)

To get an idea of what a transformed graph looks like, identify a few key points on the graph and apply the transformations to those points. What would be the key points on our \(f(x)\) graph? You might find that some points are not so informative with certain transformations.

**Things to think about**

## Warm-up solution

Here is a graph of a function, \(f(x)\).

> [figure: Cubic shaped graph crossing the x-axis at -1 and touching it at 2, and crossing the y-axis at 4 — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/order-order/images/original-fx.svg`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

For each of the following transformations, sketch the transformed graph and write its equation in terms of \(f\).

Translation by \(\begin{pmatrix}-2\\0\end{pmatrix}\)

This is a translation to the left by \(2\) units.

> [figure: The translated graph crosses the x-axis at -3, has its local maximum at (-2,4) and its local minimum at the origin — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/order-order/images/fx-1.svg`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

Algebraically, when translating \(2\) units left we replace \(x\) with \(x+2\), so we can write \[y=f(x+2).\]

The graph is translated \(4\) units downwards.

> [figure: The translated graph has its local maximum at the origin and its local minimum at (2,-4) — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/order-order/images/fx-2.svg`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

We can write this as

\[y=f(x)-4.\]

You can think of this as replacing \(y\) with \(y+4\), which is consistent with how we treated \(x\) in the first example.

The graph is made \(3\) times as wide.

> [figure: The stretched graph still has its maximum at (0,4) and its minimum is now at (6,0) — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/order-order/images/fx-3.svg`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

We replace the \(x\) with \(\frac{x}{3}\), so we can write this as \[y=f\left(\frac{x}{3}\right).\]

The graph is made half as tall.

> [figure: The stretched graph still has its minimum where it touches the x-axis at 2 but now the maximum is at (0,2) — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/order-order/images/fx-4.svg`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

We replace \(y\) with \(2y\) and write this as \[y=\frac{1}{2}\;f(x).\]

## Main problem

What happens if we apply more than one transformation to a graph?

Choose two of these transformations and apply them in turn starting with the function \(f(x)\). Sketch the resulting graph after you have applied one transformation and then the other. Does it matter which order you apply the two transformations?

Does the order matter for all pairs, some pairs or none of the pairs?

> [figure: Cubic shaped graph crossing the x-axis at -1 and touching it at 2, and crossing the y-axis at 4 — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/order-order/images/original-fx.svg`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

Translation by \(\begin{pmatrix}-2\\0\end{pmatrix}\)

Translation by \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\-4\end{pmatrix}\)

Stretch by factor \(3\) parallel to \(x\)

Stretch by factor \(\frac{1}{2}\) parallel to \(y\)

Would your answer be different if we had chosen a different set of transformations? Or a different starting function?

## Solution

Transformations (1) and (2)

Applying (1) then (2) translates the graph \(2\) units to the left and then \(4\) units down. Applying (2) then (1) translates it down then left. The result is the same; the order does not matter.

> [figure: The transformed graph touches the x-axis at 2 and crosses at 4, and crosses the y-axis at -4 — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/order-order/images/fx-12.svg`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

One of the key points on the graph is the local maximum at \((0,4)\). Applying the transformations in either order takes this point to \((-2,0)\) as shown dotted in the diagram.

Algebraically, we replace \(x\) with \(x+2\), and replace \(y\) with \(y+4\), giving us \[y+4=f(x+2) \quad\implies\quad y=f(x+2)-4.\]

Transformations (1) and (3)

Applying (1) then (3) translates the graph \(2\) units to the left and then stretches it horizontally. The local maximum at \((0,4)\) moves to \((-2,4)\) which is then stretched away from the \(y\)-axis to \((-6,4)\).

Applying (3) to the point \((0,4)\) does not move it as it is on the \(y\)-axis. Transformation (1) then moves it to \((-2,4)\). This time, the order has made a difference to where the local maximum ends up and we get two different graphs, as shown here in blue and green.

> [figure: The result of the transformation by (1) followed by (3) is a curve which crosses the x-axis, at -9 and touches it at the origin and has a local maximum at (-6,4); The result of transformation by (3) followed by (1) is a curve which crosses the x-axis at -5 and touches it at 4 and has a local maximum at (-2,4) — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/order-order/images/fx-13.svg`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

What is it that makes the order matter this time whereas it didn’t matter for transformations (1) and (2)?

How are the two resulting graphs related? What is the transformation from one to the other?

The green and blue graphs are related by a horizontal translation through a distance of \(4\). This is the difference between a translation of \(2\), and a translation of \(2\) that is then scaled up by a factor of \(3\).

The order matters because both transformations are acting horizontally.

**The transformation**

Algebraically, transformation (1) replaces

\(x\)

with

\(x+2\)

while (3) replaces

\(x\)

with

\(\frac{x}{3}\)

. So the different orders look like this.

\[\begin{align*} y&=f(x) \quad\stackrel{(1)}{\longrightarrow}\quad y=f(x+2) \quad\stackrel{(3)}{\longrightarrow}\quad y=f\left(\frac{x}{3}+2\right) \\ y&=f(x) \quad\stackrel{(3)}{\longrightarrow}\quad y=f\left(\frac{x}{3}\right) \quad\stackrel{(1)}{\longrightarrow}\quad y=f\left(\frac{x+2}{3}\right) \end{align*}\]

Transformations (1) and (4)

> [figure: The transformed graph crosses the x-axis at -3 and touches it at the origin and has a local maximum at (-2,2) — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/order-order/images/fx-14.svg`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

The order does not matter. Algebraically we have \(y=\frac{1}{2}\,f(x+2)\).

Transformations (2) and (3)

> [figure: The transformed graph touches the x-axis at the origin and crosses it at 9, and has a local minimum at (6,-4) — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/order-order/images/fx-23.svg`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

The order does not matter. Algebraically we have \(y=f\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)-4\).

Transformations (2) and (4)

> [figure: The result of the transformation by (2) followed by (4) crosses the y-axis at -2 and has the local minimum at (2,-4); The result of transformation by (4) followed by (2) touches the x-axis at the origin and has the local minimum at (2,-2) — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/order-order/images/fx-24.svg`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

The order does matter. Algebraically, transformation (2) replaces

\(y\)

with

\(y+4\)

while (4) replaces

\(y\)

with

\(2y\)

. So the different orders look like this.

\[\begin{align*} y&=f(x) \quad\stackrel{(2)}{\longrightarrow}\quad y+4=f(x) \quad\stackrel{(4)}{\longrightarrow}\quad 2y+4=f(x) \implies y=\frac{1}{2}\big(f(x)-4\big) \\ y&=f(x) \quad\stackrel{(4)}{\longrightarrow}\quad 2y=f(x) \quad\stackrel{(2)}{\longrightarrow}\quad 2(y+4)=f(x) \implies y=\frac{1}{2}\,f(x)-4 \end{align*}\]

As before, how are the two resulting graphs related?

Transformations (3) and (4)

> [figure: The transformed graph has the local maximum where it crosses the y axis at 2 and the local minimum where it touches the x axis at 6 — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/order-order/images/fx-34.svg`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

The order does not matter. Algebraically we have \(y=\frac{1}{2}\,f\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)\).

Of our four transformations, (1) and (3) are in the \(x\) direction while (2) and (4) are in the \(y\) direction. The order matters whenever we combine a stretch and a translation in the same direction.

In each of the cases (1)(3) and (2)(4) above, the resulting graphs are related by a translation. Can you explain the magnitude of the translation in each case?

The function used in this example has the shape of a cubic. The same conclusions would be true of any other function, but notice that with simple functions such as \(f(x)=x^2\) you cannot distinguish visually between a horizontal and a vertical stretch.

**Conclusion**

How would a translation by \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\end{pmatrix}\) behave when combined with other transformations?

What if we combined three of the original transformations? Would the order always matter?

# Can we draw the graph of  $\left| x + [x] \right|$?

## Question

A function

\(f\)

is defined on

\(\mathbb{R}\)

by

\[\begin{equation*} f \colon x \to \left| x + [x] \right| \end{equation*}\]

where \([x]\) indicates the greatest integer less than or equal to \(x\), e.g. \([3] = 3\), \([2.4] = 2\), \([-3.6] = -4\). Sketch the graph of the function for \(-3 \le x \le 3\). What is the range of \(f\)? Is the mapping one-one?

The function \(g\) is defined by \(g \colon x \to \left| x + [x] \right|\), \(x \in \mathbb{R}_+\), \(x \notin \mathbb{Z}_+\). Find the rule and domain of the inverse function \(g^{-1}\).

## Solution

The function \([x]\) defined here is called the [floor function](https://undergroundmathematics.org/glossary/floor-function).

Note that the value of our function \(f(x)\) will change abruptly at each integer value of \(x\). Let’s look at the behaviour of \(f\) on [intervals](https://undergroundmathematics.org/glossary/interval-notation) like \([0,1)\), \([1,2)\), etc.

When

\(0 \le x < 1\)

, we have that

\([x] = 0\)

and so

\[\begin{equation*} f(x) = \left| x + [x] \right| = |x| = x. \end{equation*}\]

When

\(1 \le x < 2\)

, we have

\([x] = 1\)

so

\[\begin{equation*} f(x) = \left| x + [x] \right| = |x+1| = x + 1 \end{equation*}\]

and similarly for all other intervals of the form

\([n,n+1)\)

where

\(n\)

is a positive integer,

\[\begin{equation*} f(x) = x + n . \end{equation*}\]

On the other hand, when

\(-1 \le x < 0\)

, we have

\([x] = -1\)

and so

\[\begin{equation*} f(x) = \left| x + [x] \right| = |x-1| = -x + 1. \end{equation*}\]

Similarly, for all intervals of the form

\([n,n+1)\)

with

\(n < 0\)

,

\[\begin{equation*} f(x) = -x - n . \end{equation*}\]

These considerations lead to the following graph.

> [figure: graph of the function f — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/r5362/images/sketch-labelled.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

As can be seen from the graph, the range of \(f\) is \[f(x)\geq 0, f(x)\neq 1,3,5,\ldots.\]

Notice that \(f(-1)=f(1)=2\) and similarly for other non-zero integer values of \(x\). Hence the mapping is not one-to-one.

The notation \(x \in \mathbb{R}_+\), \(x \notin \mathbb{Z}_+\) means that the domain of \(g\) is the real numbers greater than zero but excluding all the positive integers. Where the question asks for the ‘rule’ it means an algebraic definition of the function.

Remember that an inverse function does not exist for a function such as \(f\) that is not one-to-one. The restricted domain of \(g\) means that it is one-to-one and does have an inverse.

Notice also that with the restricted domain, \(x+[x]\) is always positive, so the definition of \(g\) can (more conveniently) be written without the modulus sign.

By definition, the domain of \(g^{-1}\) is the same as the range of \(g\). From the graph, we can see that this is \[0<x<1\text{ and }2<x<3\text{ and }\ldots\text{ and }2n<x<2n+1\ldots\] where \(n\) is a positive integer. This can be written as \[(0,1) \cup (2,3) \cup (4,5) \ldots \cup (2n,2n+1) \cup \ldots .\]

To find the rule that defines \(g^{-1}\), let’s first think about what \(g\) is doing. We can consider the number \(x\) as being made up of two parts – the whole number part \([x]\) and its fractional part which we call \(a\) (such that \(0<a<1\)). Then \[x=[x]+a\] and \[g(x)=x+[x] = 2[x]+a.\] In other words, the function \(g\) doubles the whole number part and keeps the fractional part the same. We can think about \(g\) as a function machine.

> [figure: g as a function machine — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/r5362/images/g-machine.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

We have defined the operation ‘split’ to mean turn \(x\) into a whole number and a fractional part between \(0\) and \(1\). The operation ‘join’ is its inverse which is actually just addition.

Now we can draw the inverse function machine.

> [figure: g inverse as a function machine — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/r5362/images/g-1-machine.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

So now we see that \[g^{-1}(x)=\frac{1}{2}[x]+a = \frac{1}{2}[x]+x-[x] = x-\frac{1}{2}[x].\]

Alternatively, we are to find the function \(g^{-1}\) such that \(g^{-1}(x + [x]) = x\) whenever \(x\) is in the domain of \(g\). So we want to write \(x\) as a function of \((x+[x])\).

Thus, the required rule is \(g^{-1}(x) = x - \dfrac{[x]}{2}\), as before.

 We note that

\([x + [x]] = 2[x]\)

, so we can write

\[\begin{equation*} x = x + [x] - [x] = (x + [x]) - \frac{[x + [x]]}{2}. \end{equation*}\]

> [figure: A graph of g and its reflection in the line y = x — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/r5362/images/sketch-reflection-labelled.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

The graph of \(y = g(x)\) is in blue, the line \(y = x\) is a dashed line, and \(y=g^{-1}(x)\) is in red.

We can reply by pointing out that \(5.75\) does not lie in the domain of \(g^{-1}\), even though the rule that defines \(g^{-1}\) can be applied, in principle, to any real number.

 Suppose someone objects that

\(g^{-1}(x) = x - \dfrac{[x]}{2}\)

 is not the inverse of

\(g\)

 as, for example,

\[\begin{equation*} g(g^{-1}(5.75)) = g\left( 5.75 - \frac{[5.75]}{2} \right) = g(5.75 - 2.5) = g(3.25) = 3.25 + [3.25] = 6.25. \end{equation*}\]

# Can we sketch and describe these composite functions?

## Question

1. The functions \(f\) and \(g\) are defined by \[\begin{align*} f&: x\mapsto e^x, &&x\in\mathbb{R}, \\ g&: x\mapsto x-1, &&x\in\mathbb{R}. \end{align*}\]  Sketch in a single diagram the graphs of \(f\) and the composite functions \(gf\) and \(fg\), labelling each graph clearly.  State briefly the relationship
  1. between the graphs of \(f\) and \(gf\),
  2. between the graphs of \(f\) and \(fg\).
2. Express \((1-x)(x-3)\) in the form \(a-(x-b)^2\), where \(a\) and \(b\) are constants. State the coordinates of the maximum point on the graph of \(y=(1-x)(x-3)\), and state what symmetry the graph possesses.  Sketch the graph of \(y=e^{(1-x)(x-3)}\).

## Suggestion

How do we compose two functions together?

---

How does expressing \((1-x)(x-3)\) in the form \(a-(x-b)^2\) help us find the maximum value of \(y\)?

---

Things to look out for when sketching a curve:

- can I find the asymptotes?
- can I find the intercepts with the axes?
- can I find the stationary points and their nature?
- what happens to the curve as \(x\rightarrow \pm \infty ?\)

## Solution

First, we’ll find the composite functions \(gf\) and \(fg\). We have \[gf = e^x-1\] and \[fg = e^{x-1}.\]

Let’s first sketch \(y=e^x\). We know that \(e^x\to 0\) as \(x\to -\infty\), the graph crosses the \(y\)-axis at \((1,0)\) and it is strictly increasing. So it looks roughly like this:

> [figure: the graph of y = e to the x — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/r5595/images/sketch1.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

*\(y=e^x\)*

Now let’s add a sketch of \(e^x-1\). We know that this is a translation of \(y=e^x\) by \(-1\) in the \(y\)-direction, and that \(y=e^x\) and \(y=e^x-1\) cannot intersect. So our graph now looks like:

> [figure: the graphs of y equals e to the x and y equals e to the x - 1 — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/r5595/images/sketch2.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

*\(y=e^x\) and \(y=e^x -1\)*

Finally, we add \(y=e^{x-1}\). This is a translation of \(y=e^x\) by \(1\) in the \(x\)-direction. The graphs of \(y = e^x\) and \(y=e^{x-1}\) don’t meet, but \(y=e^{x-1}\) does meet \(y=e^x-1\). So a sketch of the three functions looks like this:

> [figure: the three graphs y equals e to the x, y equals e to the x brackets minus 1, and y = e to the brackets x minus 1 — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/r5595/images/sketch3.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).

*\(y=e^x\) and \(y=e^x -1\) and \(y=e^{(x-1)}\)*

The graph of \(gf\) is a translation of \(f\) by one unit in the negative \(y\) direction.

The graph of \(fg\) is a translation of \(f\) by one unit in the positive \(x\) direction.

We expand \((1-x)(x-3)\) to obtain \(-x^2+4x-3\).

Completing the square, we find that \((1-x)(x-3)=-x^2+4x-3=-(x-2)^2+4-3=1-(x-2)^2.\)

We could also do this by expanding both expressions and solving for \(a\) and \(b\) after comparing coefficients.

From the rewriting of the equation \(y=(1-x)(x-3)\) in the form \(y=1-(x-2)^2\), we see that the maximum point on the graph occurs when \(y=1\) because the expression \(-(x-2)^2\) must be negative or zero. The expression \(-(x-2)^2\) is \(0\) when \(x=2\) so the maximum point has coordinates \((2,1)\). The graph possesses line symmetry about \(x=2\).

So the graph

- has a maximum at \(x=2\), \(y=e\);
- has symmetry about \(x=2\);
- has its \(y\)-intercept at \(e^{-3}\);
- sees \(y\rightarrow0\) as \(x\rightarrow\pm\infty\).

The sketch is

> [figure: Sketch of y equals e to the power 1 minus bracket x minus 2 squared — `https://undergroundmathematics.org/combining-functions/r5595/images/sketch4.png`] (image not included in the text import; path of record).
